crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Pathology Detection and Scan Triage
children.blurb: Pathology detection and scan triage covers software that examines medical images for signs of disease or injury and software that orders the resulting worklist.

children.name: Synthetic Imaging from Existing Scans
children.blurb: Synthetic imaging from existing scans is the generation of new medical images that were not acquired directly from a patient, produced by models trained on archives of prior scans.

children.name: Anatomical Models and 3D Printing
children.blurb: Anatomical models and 3D printing in radiology covers patient-specific physical and digital replicas built from CT, MRI, ultrasound, and other volumetric imaging.

children.name: Point of Care Ultrasound Enhancement
children.blurb: Point of care ultrasound enhancement covers software that improves the image quality, measurement, and interpretation of ultrasound scans performed at the bedside, in emergency departments, clinics, and other non-radiology settings.

children.name: Radiomics
children.blurb: Radiomics is the extraction of quantitative features from medical images, such as CT, MRI, and PET scans, to build models that support diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment response assessment.

sections.body: Diagnostic imaging and radiology is the part of medicine where pictures of the body are made and read, and it is where artificial intelligence has moved furthest from research into daily work. Software now flags suspected strokes and brain bleeds on CT scans, marks lung nodules on chest imaging, and sorts mammograms and chest X-rays into queues so the most worrying cases reach a radiologist first. Some systems generate extra views or cleaner images from scans that already exist, and others build three dimensional models of organs from slice data. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, and imaging holds a large share of them. The work is detection, triage and measurement, not diagnosis on its own.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Triage and detection are the most mature areas, with several tools cleared for clinical use and running in hospitals, though performance measured in one hospital often drops in another because scanners, protocols and patient groups differ. Synthetic imaging is promising for training and for filling gaps in sparse data, but a generated image is not a measurement and can carry the assumptions of the model that made it. Anatomical models and 3D printing are established in surgical planning, with the automation still mostly in the segmentation step. Ultrasound enhancement helps with image quality and probe guidance, yet ultrasound remains the hardest modality to standardise. Radiomics produces far more candidate features than any study can validate, and few signatures have held up across sites. The honest limits are common to all of it: narrow tasks, weak generalisation, and little evidence yet that these tools change patient outcomes rather than just reader speed.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the path from finding a problem to measuring it. Pathology Detection and Scan Triage is the entry point, covering the systems that flag and rank abnormalities, and it is where most of the clinical evidence sits. Synthetic Imaging from Existing Scans takes the opposite direction, covering images created or improved by models rather than read by them, and it is the page to read for questions about training data and image realism. Anatomical Models and 3D Printing moves from flat images to physical and digital objects for planning and education. Point of Care Ultrasound Enhancement covers the bedside setting, where image quality is poor and the operator matters as much as the software. Radiomics closes the section by turning images into numerical features for prediction, and it is the most research bound of the five. Read together they show a field that is strong at perception and triage, and still thin on proof that any of it improves what happens to a patient.
